source: Ellis, Wong, Nye, Sable-Meyer, Cary, Morales, Hewitt, Solar-Lezama, Tenenbaum (2020/2021) DreamCoder: growing generalizable, interpretable knowledge with wake-sleep Bayesian program learning
finding: Core theory. Expertise is a library of symbolic concepts (a prior over programs) plus a neural recognition model that guides search. Both are learned by alternating wake (solve tasks), sleep-abstraction (grow library) and sleep-dreaming (train recognition net).
numbers: Training sets of 100-200 tasks per domain; 8 domains (list processing, text editing, LOGO graphics, towers, regex, symbolic regression, physics laws, recursive functions).
quote: Acquiring expertise means learning these languages -- systems of concepts, alongside the skills to use them.
limits: Framed as approximate Bayesian inference: library L is the prior, recognition net Q approximates the posterior. Domain-specific net architectures (CNN for images).
agent_relevance: The library is a memory of solved subgoals; the recognition model is a learned retrieval/ordering of which to try first. Our agent has no trainable net, so the recognition role must be played by retrieval over named helpers.

source: Ellis, Wong, Nye, Sable-Meyer, Cary, Morales, Hewitt, Solar-Lezama, Tenenbaum (2020/2021) DreamCoder: growing generalizable, interpretable knowledge with wake-sleep Bayesian program learning
finding: Abstraction phase objective: choose library additions that minimise description length of the library plus the description length of refactored solutions found in waking. This compresses out reused semantic patterns, not just repeated syntax, by searching over lambda-calculus refactorings.
numbers: Refactoring bounded by 3 beta-reduction steps; about 10^14 refactorings in the 'map' example, held in a version space of about 10^6 nodes built in minutes (explicit enumeration would take centuries).
limits: Compression is a proxy for usefulness. The paper reports library depth correlates with solve rate (r=0.79) but the objective itself does not measure future reuse.
agent_relevance: A keep-or-drop rule for helpers can be code-computed: keep a helper only if rewriting solved tasks with it shortens total size by more than its own cost. This fits guardrail G5 (code selects).

source: Ellis, Wong, Nye, Sable-Meyer, Cary, Morales, Hewitt, Solar-Lezama, Tenenbaum (2020/2021) DreamCoder: growing generalizable, interpretable knowledge with wake-sleep Bayesian program learning
finding: Dreaming differs from classic wake-sleep. Dreams are random problems drawn from the library prior, then SOLVED by the same search, and the net learns to predict those solutions. Replays of real solved tasks keep it grounded.
numbers: Recognition net trained on 100-200 real tasks plus unlimited fantasies; fantasies are called critical for data efficiency.
limits: Needs a generative model of tasks (programs executed to produce inputs). Hard to port to open-ended language tasks.
agent_relevance: Analogue for an agent: generate synthetic practice problems from the helper library, solve them, and store which helper fits which problem shape. Costly in tokens; test against plain retries (G7).

source: Ellis, Wong, Nye, Sable-Meyer, Cary, Morales, Hewitt, Solar-Lezama, Tenenbaum (2020/2021) DreamCoder: growing generalizable, interpretable knowledge with wake-sleep Bayesian program learning
finding: Text editing: before learning DreamCoder solved 3.7% of 108 SyGuS 2017 problems in 10 minutes (mean search 235 s); after learning 79.6% (mean 40 s). CVC4, best competition entry, solved 82.4% with 1 hour and 8 CPUs; DreamCoder with that budget solved 84.3%.
numbers: Trained on 128 auto-generated tasks, tested on 108 SyGuS tasks. One single learned library for all problems, versus hand-engineered primitive sets per problem in SyGuS.
limits: Single run figures given; no seed variance for this experiment in the main text. Held-out set is a different distribution from training tasks.
agent_relevance: Largest measured gain from library plus recognition is on a domain where the base language is weak. Expect gains where the plain solver lacks the right primitives, small gains where it already has them.

source: Ellis, Wong, Nye, Sable-Meyer, Cary, Morales, Hewitt, Solar-Lezama, Tenenbaum (2020/2021) DreamCoder: growing generalizable, interpretable knowledge with wake-sleep Bayesian program learning
finding: Ablation across six held-out domains: the full system solved the most held-out tasks everywhere. In LOGO graphics and tower building no alternative (no-dreaming, no-abstraction, Exploration-Compression, RobustFill neural synthesis, 24h enumeration up to 400M programs, Memorize variants) solved more than 60% while DreamCoder reached nearly 100%.
numbers: Five runs per curve, error bars one standard deviation. Typical convergence about one day on 20-100 CPUs. Mean search time 54.1 s, median 15.0 s across domains.
limits: Exact per-domain bar values are in Fig. 6A (not captured as text). Benchmarks are small synthetic domains with 100-200 tasks.
agent_relevance: Both parts (library and guidance) contributed. A library alone is weaker than library plus a search guide, so a stored helper must be paired with a way to pick it.

source: Ellis, Wong, Nye, Sable-Meyer, Cary, Morales, Hewitt, Solar-Lezama, Tenenbaum (2020/2021) DreamCoder: growing generalizable, interpretable knowledge with wake-sleep Bayesian program learning
finding: Memorize baselines (add whole solutions as primitives, no compression) did worse than compression-based library learning; the paper uses them to show that compression, not mere storage of solutions, is what helps.
numbers: Memorize variants run with and without the recognition model; results in Fig. S13 (not read as numbers).
limits: Only tested in the program-synthesis domains of the paper. Differences between compress and memorise are given as plots.
agent_relevance: Direct warning for a memory of solved subgoals: storing raw past solutions is not the same as storing abstracted, parameterised helpers.

source: Ellis, Wong, Nye, Sable-Meyer, Cary, Morales, Hewitt, Solar-Lezama, Tenenbaum (2020/2021) DreamCoder: growing generalizable, interpretable knowledge with wake-sleep Bayesian program learning
finding: Library depth and size track performance: deeper libraries correlated with more tasks solved (r=0.79 across domains and cycles). A recognition model gives better performance at every depth and builds deeper libraries.
numbers: Each dot a single wake/sleep cycle in a single run in a single domain; size effect weaker than depth effect.
limits: Correlational over training trajectories, not a controlled manipulation of depth.
agent_relevance: Hierarchical reuse (helpers built from helpers) is where gains accumulate; a flat bag of helpers may not.

source: Ellis, Wong, Nye, Sable-Meyer, Cary, Morales, Hewitt, Solar-Lezama, Tenenbaum (2020/2021) DreamCoder: growing generalizable, interpretable knowledge with wake-sleep Bayesian program learning
finding: Starting from generic primitives only, DreamCoder learned 93% of 60 physics laws and identities after 8 wake/sleep cycles, first building vector algebra (inner product, sum, norm) then an inverse-square-law schema reused for gravitation and Coulomb's law.
numbers: 60 laws from AP and MCAT cheat sheets, data given as numeric examples; Planck units.
limits: Equations given as numbers; no noise or distractor analysis in main text.
agent_relevance: Shows a library can change the basis of representation, which is the concept-formation step our agent would need.

source: Ellis, Wong, Nye, Sable-Meyer, Cary, Morales, Hewitt, Solar-Lezama, Tenenbaum (2020/2021) DreamCoder: growing generalizable, interpretable knowledge with wake-sleep Bayesian program learning
finding: Learning a language from near nothing: given 1959-Lisp primitives plus the Y-combinator, DreamCoder solved all 20 intro CS tasks and rediscovered fold and unfold, then map, filter, zip, length, i.e. the 'origami' basis, in order.
numbers: About five days on 64 CPUs for this experiment.
limits: Only 20 tasks and a very high compute budget; the order of discovery was inspected by hand.
agent_relevance: Existence proof that helpers can be grown bottom-up, but at a compute cost far above our token budgets.

source: Ellis, Wong, Nye, Sable-Meyer, Cary, Morales, Hewitt, Solar-Lezama, Tenenbaum (2020/2021) DreamCoder: growing generalizable, interpretable knowledge with wake-sleep Bayesian program learning
finding: List-processing and LOGO libraries were interpretable: about 20 new routines for list tasks (filter, max, nth largest, sort built in layers); LOGO learned polygon, circle, spiral and a higher-order radial-symmetry routine.
numbers: 218 list problems split 50/50 train/test with 15 examples each; 160 LOGO images split 50/50; 20 wake/sleep cycles.
limits: Interpretability judged qualitatively by the authors, no human study.
agent_relevance: Names a person or model can read matter later (see LILO AutoDoc).

source: Ellis, Wong, Nye, Sable-Meyer, Cary, Morales, Hewitt, Solar-Lezama, Tenenbaum (2020/2021) DreamCoder: growing generalizable, interpretable knowledge with wake-sleep Bayesian program learning
finding: Recognition network activations became aligned with the structure of the final programs: correlation between task similarity in net space and similarity in code components rose over learning (p < 10^-4, chi-square, pre vs post).
numbers: Fig. S4; t-SNE only qualitative.
limits: Interpretive link to expert chunking in humans is speculation.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that retrieval keys should come from solution structure, not surface text of problems.

source: Bowers, Olausson, Wong, Grand, Tenenbaum, Ellis, Solar-Lezama (2023) Top-down synthesis for library learning (Stitch)
finding: Stitch replaces DreamCoder's bottom-up version-space compression with corpus-guided top-down search for lambda-abstractions, pruned by an upper bound on achievable compression. It is an anytime algorithm.
numbers: 3-4 orders of magnitude faster (1,000-10,000x) and 2 orders of magnitude less memory than DreamCoder's compression, with equal or better compression on DreamCoder's own benchmarks.
limits: Compression ratio is the quality metric, not downstream solve rate.
agent_relevance: Cheap enough to re-derive the whole library each round, so early bad helpers can be dropped. The idea of an upper bound for pruning is transferable to code that scores candidate helpers.

source: Bowers, Olausson, Wong, Grand, Tenenbaum, Ellis, Solar-Lezama (2023) Top-down synthesis for library learning (Stitch)
finding: Large-scale test on eight 2D CAD domains: test-set compression ratio 2.55x (castles) to 11.57x (nuts and bolts) in 0.24 s to 77 s with 11 MB to 684 MB peak memory; 50 random splits. DreamCoder could not run even on nuts and bolts with 256 GB RAM and hours.
numbers: Table 2: e.g. gadgets 3.91 test, furniture 4.85, vehicles 4.14, bridges 3.78, cities 3.06, houses 8.85; train and test ratios close.
limits: Compression on synthetic CAD domains with ground-truth programs, not on programs that a solver found.
agent_relevance: Train and test compression were close, so abstractions found were not overfit to the training corpus.

source: Bowers, Olausson, Wong, Grand, Tenenbaum, Ellis, Solar-Lezama (2023) Top-down synthesis for library learning (Stitch)
finding: Pruning ablation: with all pruning off Stitch finds no abstraction within the budget (50 GB, 90 min) in any of the eight domains; the corpus-guided pruning is what makes top-down search tractable. Disabling argument-capture pruning hits the memory limit on more than half the domains.
numbers: Max arity 3; nodes explored counted for determinism.
limits: Single-abstraction first iteration only.
agent_relevance: Cost of abstraction search explodes without a score bound; any helper-mining step in the agent must be bounded and anytime.

source: Grand, Wong, Bowers, Olausson, Liu, Tenenbaum, Andreas (2024) LILO: learning interpretable libraries by compressing and documenting code
finding: LILO loop: an LLM (Codex code-davinci-002) plus enumerative search solve tasks, Stitch compresses solved programs into abstractions, and an LLM (gpt-3.5-turbo) writes names and docstrings (AutoDoc) for each abstraction, which go back into the next prompt.
numbers: Benchmarks: REGEX, CLEVR (scene reasoning), LOGO. Up to 4 prompts per task, 4 completions per prompt; library re-derived from the base DSL every iteration.
limits: Needs natural-language task descriptions. Codex was in a free researcher beta; costs are estimated with gpt-3.5 prices.
agent_relevance: This is the closest published pattern to our memory-of-subgoals idea: compress, then name and document so a model can use it.

source: Grand, Wong, Bowers, Olausson, Liu, Tenenbaum, Andreas (2024) LILO: learning interpretable libraries by compressing and documenting code
finding: Online solve rates (mean test %, REGEX / CLEVR / LOGO): DreamCoder 43.93 / 94.50 / 28.53; LLM Solver 76.13 / 88.67 / 32.13; LLM Solver plus search 76.60 / 96.44 / 37.84; LILO 77.07 / 96.76 / 48.95.
numbers: 3 seeds. Std for LILO: 14.14, 3.12, 9.46; for LLM solver on REGEX 12.04. Max LILO: 93.20 / 99.03 / 73.87.
limits: On REGEX and CLEVR the difference between LILO and the LLM solver with search is under 1 point and well inside seed noise; the clear library gain is LOGO (+11.1 over solver+search).
agent_relevance: Most of the lift over DreamCoder comes from the LLM, not the library. Credit a library only when it beats a strong plain-LLM arm at equal tokens (G7).

source: Grand, Wong, Bowers, Olausson, Liu, Tenenbaum, Andreas (2024) LILO: learning interpretable libraries by compressing and documenting code
finding: Giving the LLM raw Stitch abstractions with anonymous names (fn_42) HURT: solve-rate change versus plain LLM solver of -30.60 (REGEX), -2.91 (CLEVR), -11.11 (LOGO). Adding AutoDoc recovered +9.73 (REGEX), +2.27 (CLEVR), 0.00 (LOGO).
numbers: Mean test solve rates over 3 runs. LILO(-Search / -AutoDoc) vs LILO(-Search).
quote: providing the LLM with abstractions did not help--and in some cases, significantly hurt
limits: On LOGO AutoDoc did not help; authors blame semantic errors in generated docstrings (wrong names for what a function does).
agent_relevance: Key finding for us: an undocumented helper library can lower accuracy. Any helper we store must carry a readable name, signature and a usage example, and the docs must be checked by running (G8).

source: Grand, Wong, Bowers, Olausson, Liu, Tenenbaum, Andreas (2024) LILO: learning interpretable libraries by compressing and documenting code
finding: Offline test with the final library and plain enumerative search, no language: DreamCoder library +19.6 (REGEX), +62.46 (CLEVR), +29.73 (LOGO) over the base DSL; LILO library +42.27, +63.43, +43.24 over base. LILO libraries beat libraries derived post hoc from LLM-solver runs.
numbers: Table 1 lower: LILO mean 64.27 / 92.56 / 41.14 vs DreamCoder 41.60 / 91.59 / 30.63 on REGEX / CLEVR / LOGO (seed std up to 8.66).
limits: Offline test is where library quality is isolated from the LLM; one dataset family, three DSLs.
agent_relevance: The library itself, apart from the model, carries real value on held-out tasks, but only moderately above DreamCoder on CLEVR (+1 point).

source: Grand, Wong, Bowers, Olausson, Liu, Tenenbaum, Andreas (2024) LILO: learning interpretable libraries by compressing and documenting code
finding: Cost: one LILO training iteration costs about as much as an 1800 s enumerative search on 96 CPUs (about 48 CPU-hours). LLM search took 0.8M-1.2M GPT tokens per iteration.
numbers: Table 6 (dollars per iteration): LILO $1.77 / $1.87 / $2.01 vs DreamCoder $1.16 / $0.71 / $2.07 (REGEX / CLEVR / LOGO). c5.24xlarge at $4.08/h; gpt-3.5-turbo at $0.002 per 1K tokens.
limits: Prices change; Codex search itself was free during the study.
agent_relevance: Setup and re-learning cost per round is millions of tokens. Our agent must count this cost against any benefit (G7).

source: Grand, Wong, Bowers, Olausson, Liu, Tenenbaum, Andreas (2024) LILO: learning interpretable libraries by compressing and documenting code
finding: Asking GPT-4 to do the compression itself failed: only 19.01% (998 of 5250) of generated abstractions were valid expressions (REGEX 24.93%, CLEVR 24.20%, LOGO 4.93%), compressivity hovered near 1.0x, and abstractions were shorter and trivial compared with Stitch.
numbers: Best-effort prompt engineering, authors say it took a lot of effort and gave only negative results.
limits: Tested with GPT-4 (2023); newer models may do better.
agent_relevance: Keep compression in code, not in the model. Matches our rule that the program counts and compares while the model fills slots.

source: Grand, Wong, Bowers, Olausson, Liu, Tenenbaum, Andreas (2024) LILO: learning interpretable libraries by compressing and documenting code
finding: Enumerative search added most on LOGO, which needs domain-specific structures such as snowflake and staircase that language alone does not give. LLM search was faster in wall clock than enumerative search.
numbers: LILO(-Search) LOGO mean 21.02 vs LILO 48.95.
limits: LOGO has the highest seed variance (std 9-21).
agent_relevance: LLM guess plus a non-LLM search over the library is complementary; a code-run fallback search may be worth keeping.

source: Wong, Ellis, Tenenbaum, Andreas (2021) Leveraging language to learn program abstractions and search heuristics (LAPS)
finding: LAPS adds natural-language task descriptions to DreamCoder: language guides which abstractions to keep (language-program compression) and trains a neural search model from a translation model. Language is used in training only; test-time language is optional.
numbers: Domains: strings (n_test=500), graphics LOGO (111 test), scenes (115 test).
limits: Synthetic and human language annotations; human-language results are lower.
agent_relevance: Names and descriptions as retrieval keys for helpers is a published idea with data.

source: Wong, Ellis, Tenenbaum, Andreas (2021) Leveraging language to learn program abstractions and search heuristics (LAPS)
finding: Held-out solve rates, synthetic language (strings / graphics mean / scenes mean): DreamCoder no language 33.4 / 42.64 / 73.9; LAPS in neural search 52.2 / 52.93 / 88.1; LAPS plus mutual exclusivity plus language-program compression 54.6 / 81.98 / 95.9.
numbers: Graphics best-of-replications: 49.55 for DreamCoder vs 98.19 for the full LAPS. With human language at train and test: 48.6 strings, 58.55 graphics, 95.6 scenes.
limits: Large gap between best and mean on graphics for DreamCoder and weaker LAPS variants (seed instability). Human-language graphics falls to 58.55.
agent_relevance: Language helps most when search is hard (graphics); gain is smaller when the base solver is already strong (scenes).

source: Wong, Ellis, Tenenbaum, Andreas (2021) Leveraging language to learn program abstractions and search heuristics (LAPS)
finding: Library quality without language at test: Original DSL with enumeration solved 0.06 / 0.00 / 27.8 (strings / graphics / scenes); DreamCoder's best library 27.2 / 41.44 / 53.6; LAPS best library 33.2 / 62.16 / 93.04. Adding example-only neural synthesis gave 52.4 / 91.0 / 95.6.
numbers: Single best library per method.
limits: Library and search model measured as separate contributions; 'best' picks the best seed.
agent_relevance: Even without language at inference, a learned library lifts solve rate far above the bare language; a good library is portable.

source: Berlot-Attwell, Rudzicz, Si (2024) Library learning doesn't: the curious case of the single-use library
finding: Direct reuse of learned tools in LEGO-Prover is nearly absent. On the released logs only 1,233 lemmas (6%) reached the final prover prompt, exactly one lemma was reused verbatim and only once, and none was reused twice. Name-level reuse was similarly rare.
numbers: Table 1 splits: valid+GPT 127 solved, 374 lemmas in prompts; valid+Human 135 solved, 265; test+GPT 111, 255; test+Human 122, 339. Over 20,000 lemmas learned in total.
limits: Analysis covers released prover logs only (not the unreleased evolver logs). Indirect reuse as in-context examples is not ruled out.
agent_relevance: Strong caution: a library that grows does not mean helpers are reused. Log helper reuse per task and report it.

source: Berlot-Attwell, Rudzicz, Si (2024) Library learning doesn't: the curious case of the single-use library
finding: Ablating all cross-problem sharing in LEGO-Prover (each theorem gets its own state) solved only 1 question fewer than the full system, using GPT-4o-mini on a random 12-problem miniF2F-valid subset with 50 attempts per problem, 2 trials.
numbers: N=12 problems, 2 trials; Figure 1 curves overlap within one standard deviation.
limits: Tiny sample, a different LLM than the original (GPT-3.5-Turbo deprecated).
agent_relevance: The reported LEGO-Prover gain (47.1% to 50.4% in its own ablation) may come from the retry and self-correction machinery rather than the library.

source: Berlot-Attwell, Rudzicz, Si (2024) Library learning doesn't: the curious case of the single-use library
finding: TroVE on MATH: its final library held only 15 functions, from 3 of 7 subject splits; only 2 were reused in correct solutions (is_perfect_square once, is_prime twice), i.e. 3 successful reuses in 3,201 test questions. A no-reuse ablation matched it: count 0.250 vs 0.236, number 0.290 vs 0.258, geometry 0.050 vs 0.058, intermediate algebra 0.134 vs 0.120.
numbers: Reproduced TroVE within 2% of the reported accuracy, 5 trials, Bonferroni-corrected one-sided Welch tests on the ablation.
quote: self-correction and self-consistency are the primary drivers of the observed performance gains
limits: Authors state the gains come from self-correction and self-consistency (generate 15 solutions, majority vote), not from reuse; they do not test all LLM library methods.
agent_relevance: The measured advantage of LLM library systems may be sampling and voting in disguise. Always compare a library arm with a same-sample-count plain arm (G4, G7).

source: Wang, Neubig, Fried (2024) TroVE: inducing verifiable and efficient toolboxes for solving programmatic tasks
finding: TroVE is training-free: the LM chooses among skip, create and import modes; it uses, grows and periodically trims a toolbox of functions. Reported: 30-120% higher accuracy than primitive-only programs across 7 MATH datasets, and 79-98% smaller toolboxes than the instance-level baseline.
numbers: 11 datasets across MATH, table QA (TabMWP, WTQ, HiTab) and GQA; CodeLlama-7B and GPT results; human verification 31% faster and 13% more accurate.
limits: Reported by authors; later reanalysis (a26) found the library rarely reused on MATH.
agent_relevance: Periodic trimming of low-use helpers is a cheap, code-run idea that avoids a bloated library.

source: Wang, Neubig, Fried (2024) TroVE: inducing verifiable and efficient toolboxes for solving programmatic tasks
finding: Untrimmed libraries hurt: the instance-level baseline created hundreds to thousands of functions and scored below primitive-only programs on most table QA sets; on GQA it dropped 0.21 in correctness against primitive; 395 functions were created and most were invalid.
numbers: Figures compare TroVE with and without trimming; the no-trim variant grows much larger.
limits: Conjecture of authors (too many low-utility options confuse the model), not tested separately.
agent_relevance: Library size is itself a cost to the model: more options in the prompt lowers accuracy. Cap and prune.

source: Stengel-Eskin, Prasad, Bansal (2024) ReGAL: refactoring programs to discover generalizable abstractions
finding: ReGAL clusters training programs, has GPT-3.5 propose helper functions by refactoring, verifies them by running, and edits or prunes them. Across five datasets the helper library raised accuracy of CodeLlama-13B by 11.5 (LOGO), 26.1 (Date) and 8.1 points (TextCraft).
numbers: Table 1 (3 seeds): CodeLlama-13B LOGO 45.6 to 57.1, Date 42.8 to 68.9, TextCraft 18.8 to 26.9; trained on about 200 examples.
limits: Gains are uneven: CodeLlama-7B LOGO 34.5 to 34.5 (0); Lemur-70B on TabMWP 27.5 to 25.7; CodeLlama-13B TabMWP 29.1 to 27.9 (slight drops). Math domains have no clear domain language.
agent_relevance: A library helps most where a task family has repeated structure and a weak base model; it can slightly hurt on strong models or on open-ended math.

source: Stengel-Eskin, Prasad, Bansal (2024) ReGAL: refactoring programs to discover generalizable abstractions
finding: Ablation on dev with CodeLlama-13B: full REGAL LOGO 55.0, Date 77.0; removing retrial dropped LOGO to 48.3 and Date to 51.9; removing the curriculum gave 36.3 and 56.6; removing pruning 52.0 and 65.5; removing code-bank editing 53.3 and 69.6.
numbers: 3 seeds. Curriculum means ordering clusters shortest query first.
limits: Dev splits only; single base model.
agent_relevance: Execution-verified retries and an easy-to-hard order of what is learned are the largest contributors; we can use both with no training.

source: Wang, Xin, Zheng et al. (2023) LEGO-Prover: neural theorem proving with growing libraries
finding: A growing library of verified Isabelle lemmas, with a prover that retrieves skills and an evolver that creates and transforms new ones. Reported pass rates: miniF2F-valid 57.0% (from 52.4%) and miniF2F-test 50.0% with 100 attempts, ChatGPT.
numbers: Earlier best: 48.0% / 45.5% (Thor plus expert iteration), 52.4% / 45.5% (Subgoal-Learning). Own ablation (50 attempts, valid): 50.4% with library vs 47.1% without. Skills source: 10.8% prover, 38.2% evolver solve-request, 51.1% evolver transformations.
limits: Library ablation is a 3.3-point gain under 50 attempts on one split. Berlot-Attwell et al. (a24, a25) found direct reuse near zero and a no-sharing ablation matched it.
agent_relevance: The 3.3-point gain is small and was later challenged; do not count it as support for a persistent lemma store without our own reuse count.

source: Cao, Kunkel, Nandi, Willsey, Tatlock, Polikarpova (2023) babble: learning better abstractions with e-graphs and anti-unification
finding: Library learning modulo theory: use e-graphs and equality saturation so programs that are equal under a given equational theory are matched, making compression robust to syntactic variation; claims better compression orders of magnitude faster than DreamCoder.
numbers: On DreamCoder's compression tasks babble beat DreamCoder; the Stitch paper reports babble 10-100x faster than DreamCoder while Stitch is 1,000-10,000x.
limits: Needs a hand-written domain theory of rewrites; babble is not anytime (Stitch paper).
agent_relevance: Two solutions with the same structure but different surface form can share one helper only if equivalence is known. Matching helpers by behaviour (running) is the cheap version.

source: Ellis, Morales, Sable-Meyer, Solar-Lezama, Tenenbaum (2018) Learning libraries of subroutines for neurally-guided Bayesian program induction (EC2)
finding: Predecessor of DreamCoder: learns a DSL while training a neural net to guide search; tested on list functions, text editing and symbolic regression and shows a library of reusable components.
numbers: Abstract page only; no numbers on the abstract page.
limits: Only the abstract was read, so detailed figures are not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Confirms the library plus neural guide pairing existed before 2020.

source: Wong, Grand, Lew, Goodman, Mansinghka, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2022) Identifying concept libraries from language about object structure
finding: People described about 2,000 procedurally generated objects. Treating naming as a search over program libraries, human lexicons favoured concise descriptions of each object while keeping the lexicon small.
numbers: About 2,000 objects; only the abstract page was seen, participant numbers not recorded.
limits: Abstract only. Used by Stitch as the 2D CAD benchmark.
agent_relevance: Human evidence that concept libraries trade description length against library size, the same trade the compression objective makes.

source: AbstractBeam authors (2024) AbstractBeam: enhancing bottom-up program synthesis using library learning
finding: Adds DreamCoder-style abstraction learning to LambdaBeam (neural bottom-up synthesis). On handwritten tasks AbstractBeam solved 53.6% vs LambdaBeam 50.2% (fold 1) and 39.6% vs 36.0% (fold 2); no gain on synthetic tasks.
numbers: 200 tasks (100 handwritten, 100 synthetic), 2-fold cross-validation, 5 runs, p < 0.05 for handwritten gains. Time on shared solved handwritten tasks 2.57 s vs 4.57 s.
limits: Authors call the gains slight; abstractions learned on handwritten tasks did not transfer to the synthetic distribution; library learning works only if abstractions exist in the domain.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: where tasks share no structure, library learning gives nothing. Check for shared structure before building a store.

source: ccocks (2025) arc_agi GitHub project (DreamCoder-inspired ARC system)
finding: A project claims an LLM-assisted program-synthesis system with a growing library for ARC, with 77.1% on ARC-AGI-1 and 26.0% on ARC-AGI-2.
numbers: Self-reported, seen only in a search summary.
limits: Unverified, not a paper, not opened.
agent_relevance: Treat as a lead only; do not rely on it.
